section_summary: This section documents U.S. and British efforts in early 1941 to limit Japan’s accumulation of petroleum and other strategic materials, especially through tanker control, export licensing, and restrictions on oil drums and storage tanks. It also covers exports of aluminum, fats, bearings, jute bags, asbestos, lard, and toluol, alongside correspondence urging a broader embargo against Japan. The final documents report German machinery and military-related goods entering Manchuria and provide intelligence on Japan’s severe asbestos shortage.

subfiles.title: Universal Oil Products cover letter concerning the Japan Gasoline Company
subfiles.from: S. R. Wilson, Universal Oil Products Company
subfiles.to: H. W. Moseley, Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Transmits R. L. Gilpatric’s January 21 letter about the Japan Gasoline Company.
subfiles.summary: Wilson forwards the enclosed Gilpatric letter at Hiram J. Halle’s request. He notes that Halle had read the letter to Moseley during a telephone conversation that morning.

subfiles.title: Gilpatric letter on settlement terms in the Japan Gasoline dispute
subfiles.about: Reports a Japanese proposal limiting requests for gasoline-process information in exchange for suspending litigation.
subfiles.summary: Yamaoka reported cables from Saneyoshi responding to Morishima’s December 5 proposal. Saneyoshi would forgo information on iso-octane processes and limit requests to sulfuric-acid alkylation, isomerization, and related catalysts for ordinary motor fuel. If Universal Oil Products and the State Department accepted, he offered to suspend the litigation for two years pending an earlier settlement.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Louis E. Berry’s activities in Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a report concerning metallurgical expert Louis E. Berry’s activities in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet cross-references a Justice Department letter transmitting a report on Louis E. Berry. The original was filed under 894.00/1001.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Ambassador Nomura’s embargo warning
subfiles.about: References a memorandum reporting Nomura’s warning about the consequences of continued American embargoes.
subfiles.summary: The referenced memorandum records Ambassador Nomura’s statement to Hull that Japan’s military group might feel forced toward further naval or military action. The warning was tied to continuation of American embargoes.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on limiting rubber exports to Japan
subfiles.about: References a telegram about a regional arrangement limiting rubber exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The telegram reported that French Indochina, the Netherlands East Indies, and Malaya were concluding an arrangement on rubber exports. Shipments would be limited to Japan’s established home-consumption requirements.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning transactions involving Prieto
subfiles.about: References another file concerning sales or proposals involving a person named Prieto.
subfiles.summary: Most of the subject and filing information is illegible in the OCR. The surviving text appears to concern sales or proposals made to Rubén Prieto and directs the reader to another file.

subfiles.title: Telegram on aluminum tanks being shipped from Manzanillo to Dairen
subfiles.about: Reports plans to break up four aluminum tanks for shipment to Dairen.
subfiles.summary: Four large aluminum tanks that reached Manzanillo in February were being cut into smaller pieces for shipment to Dairen, Manchukuo. The tanks would yield six tons of aluminum, shipped by La Consolidada of Mexico City to the shipper’s order.

subfiles.title: Message about a Richfield Oil Company meeting with the Secretary of State
subfiles.from: Mr. Brown, Office of the Secretary
subfiles.about: Requests preparation of a memorandum for a meeting on petroleum exports to the Far East.
subfiles.summary: At Colonel Patrick Hurley’s instance, Richfield Oil Company president Charles S. Jones was scheduled to see the Secretary on January 14. The expected subject was petroleum-product exports to the Far East, and a briefing memorandum was requested.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of conversation on Japanese oil stocks, quotas, and tankers
subfiles.about: Records British proposals to restrict Japan’s oil reserves by controlling quotas and tanker availability.
subfiles.summary: Neville Butler and P. C. Hill urged U.S. cooperation in discouraging Standard-Vacuum from accepting increased Japanese quotas and using its foreign-flag tankers in the Japan trade. Hornbeck obtained figures showing Standard’s proposed quota totaled 99,200 tons and that it used only two tankers between Japan and the Netherlands East Indies. He stressed the delicacy of petroleum restrictions and recalled earlier British and Dutch warnings about provoking damaging repercussions. An addendum records Hill’s estimate that Shell’s increased quota was about 140,000 tons.

subfiles.title: Handwritten calculations of Standard-Vacuum’s Japanese quota
subfiles.about: Calculates petroleum-product figures associated with Standard-Vacuum’s proposed Japanese quota.
subfiles.summary: The note records figures for gasoline, kerosene, and heavy oils and totals them at 99,200 tons. It appears to support the January 6 memorandum of conversation.

subfiles.title: British memorandum titled “Oil—Japan”
subfiles.about: Urges prompt agreement on restricting Japanese oil imports through tanker control.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum argues that increased Japanese distribution quotas for Standard and Shell would require additional company tanker tonnage and enlarge Japan’s oil intake. It warns that the supplies could strengthen discriminatory Japanese oil marketing in China and undermine Standard, Shell, and Caltex policy there. Britain also needed scarce tanker tonnage for its own war requirements and therefore sought a prompt State Department decision on the tanker-curtailment proposals.

subfiles.title: Table of U.S. petroleum-product exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Compares monthly U.S. petroleum exports to Japan in 1939 and August–November 1940.
subfiles.summary: The table lists crude oil, fuel oils, aviation gasoline, other gasoline, lubricating oil, greases, and paraffin wax. It shows especially large increases in non-aviation gasoline and lubricating oil during the 1940 comparison period.

subfiles.title: Table of Japanese petroleum imports
subfiles.about: Presents Japanese petroleum-import totals and the effect of the Batavia agreement.
subfiles.summary: The table gives Japanese petroleum-import figures for several prewar years, though some headings are lost in the OCR. A note states that the Batavia agreement would provide 1.8 million tons annually from the Netherlands East Indies, approximately 14.5 million barrels or 42.4 percent of 1939 imports.

subfiles.title: Instruction on licensing metal drums and liquid containers
subfiles.to: Collector of Customs, New York, and other collectors
subfiles.about: Explains which metal drums and containers were exempt from or subject to export licensing.
subfiles.summary: The instruction temporarily exempts small containers, certain intermediate-sized containers, and containers holding specified chemicals from the February 4 iron-and-steel export order. Other liquid containers required licenses after February 15, and petroleum licenses did not independently authorize the export of their drums. Unlimited licenses had been issued for qualifying exports to the British Empire.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter advocating tanker restrictions
subfiles.about: Urges U.S. action against American-owned foreign-flag tankers and increased oil deliveries to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Butler encloses information on Panamanian and Philippine tankers sailing to Japan and argues that restricting Japanese chartering would reduce oil-stock accumulation without directly provoking Japan. He also asks that Standard Oil be discouraged from accepting increased quotas, with Shell following parallel British guidance. Because gasoline and lubricants traveled mainly in steel drums on cargo vessels, he suggests that drum exports might also be licensed.

subfiles.title: List of tanker sailings to Japan from U.S. ports
subfiles.about: Lists November and December tanker departures for Japan and their owners.
subfiles.summary: The list identifies eight Panamanian tankers and one Philippine tanker associated with departures from Philadelphia and New York. It distinguishes vessels connected with U.S. owners from those under Norwegian or Greek ownership.

subfiles.title: British Embassy letter on Japanese purchases of oil-storage tanks
subfiles.about: Warns that Japan was rapidly expanding permanent oil-storage capacity with tanks imported from the United States.
subfiles.summary: Butler estimates that tanks shipped since December 1 supplied about two million barrels of capacity, with another million barrels shipped in October and November. The increase suggested that Japan was importing oil faster than current consumption and intended to enlarge its reserves. He asks whether the United States was considering restrictions on structural-steel storage tanks not clearly covered by the December 10 order.

subfiles.title: List of oil-storage tank shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Lists major steel storage tanks shipped from U.S. Pacific ports since December 1, 1940.
subfiles.summary: The enclosure identifies shipments aboard the Florida Maru, Terukawa Maru, Tosei Maru, Kimikawa Maru, and Yawata Maru. The listed tanks totaled approximately 1,957,000 barrels of capacity, including tanks for Japan and Mitsubishi at Qingdao.

subfiles.title: Maritime Commission consultation on foreign tanker chartering
subfiles.about: Reports that Maritime Commission officials might discourage American owners from chartering foreign-flag tankers to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Robeson and Wilcox of the Maritime Commission’s Emergency Division believed an arrangement with American tanker owners might be possible. Before acting, they requested an expression of the State Department’s interest.

subfiles.title: Cover memorandum to Welles on withdrawing tankers from Japanese use
subfiles.about: Forwards a proposal for informal approaches to oil companies controlling tankers used in the Japan trade.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum states that Far Eastern Affairs considered the possible withdrawal of American- and foreign-owned tankers from Japanese use. It recommends asking oil companies voluntarily to find non-Japanese cargoes for their vessels.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on tanker shipments of petroleum products to Japan
subfiles.about: Recommends confidential approaches to American oil companies controlling foreign-flag tankers.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports 388 American-flag tankers and 217 foreign-flag tankers controlled by American interests. It identifies seven oil companies likely to own relevant foreign-flag vessels and proposes asking them to seek alternative employment. Coordinated British and American withholding of tankers would hinder Japan’s oil imports while producing less resentment than a direct prohibition on Japanese purchases.

subfiles.title: International Communications comments on gaps in tanker restrictions
subfiles.from: Thomas Burke, Division of International Communications
subfiles.about: Notes that voluntary tanker controls would not fully restrict Japanese oil imports.
subfiles.summary: Burke concurs with the Far Eastern Affairs recommendations but observes that companies could still carry oil in their own uncontrolled tankers. He also recommends considering restrictions on gasoline and lubricating oil shipped in drums aboard ordinary cargo vessels. Owners might resist leaving the relatively safe Japan trade unless satisfactory alternative employment existed.

subfiles.title: Duplicate memorandum on gaps in proposed tanker restrictions
subfiles.from: Thomas Burke, Division of International Communications
subfiles.about: Duplicate copy of the memorandum assessing weaknesses in proposed tanker controls.
subfiles.summary: This copy repeats Burke’s warning that foreign-flag tanker measures and Maritime Commission controls would leave important gaps. It highlights company-owned tankers, drummed petroleum cargo, and owners’ possible preference for safe Japanese employment.

subfiles.title: Feis routing note requesting a reply to Clayton
subfiles.about: Requests a draft reply explaining how a matter raised by Clayton would be handled in a prospective export-control order.
subfiles.summary: Feis asks that a response to William L. Clayton be prepared for his signature. The reply was to explain how the pending order would address the products in question.

subfiles.title: Inquiry to Yost about withheld export licenses
subfiles.about: Asks why licenses for specified exports to Japan were not being issued and whether normal-quantity limits had been considered.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs requests the basis for withholding licenses on several listed commodities. It asks specifically whether the normal-quantity formula could be applied instead of a complete refusal.

subfiles.title: Clayton letter on exports of fats to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a memorandum about fats exported to Japan and questions whether they might be reaching Germany.
subfiles.summary: Clayton calls Feis’s attention to the enclosed February 26 memorandum. He speculates that some of the exported fats might be moving through Japan to Germany.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on exports of oils and fats to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports large shipments of coconut oil, salad oil, and lard to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Commerce official C. E. Lund reported exports of about eighteen million pounds of coconut oil and 400,000 pounds of salad oil. American President Lines had also asked about loading seven million pounds of lard already at the dock. Because animal oils were not normally part of the Japanese diet, Groggins questioned the shipment’s final use or destination.

subfiles.title: Feis reply to Clayton on controls over fats and oils
subfiles.about: Explains new and prospective export controls on oils and fats destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Feis states that coconut oil, copra, palm oil, palm kernels, and vegetable-oil fatty acids became subject to licensing on March 10. No licenses were being issued for their export to Japan. He adds that the Department had recommended controls on remaining fats and oils and expected further action shortly.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Herron’s call about lubricating oil in wooden barrels
subfiles.about: Records information that Japanese buyers were seeking lubricating oil packed in new oak barrels.
subfiles.summary: California Texas Oil Company president Howard M. Herron reported that brokers nationwide were being asked to ship lubricating oil in wooden barrels. His company had been asked to quote on 22,000 barrels but had refused to do so.

subfiles.title: Timken letter announcing refusal of Japanese and Russian bearing orders
subfiles.about: Explains Timken’s decision to stop bearing sales to Japan and Russia.
subfiles.summary: Timken had received no definite government guidance after asking whether bearing exports to Japan and Russia were viewed unfavorably. The company nevertheless refused new Japanese inquiries, canceled $250,000 in Japanese orders and $26,984 in Russian orders, and barred future sales to either country. Timken regarded bearings as an indirect export of nickel and as assistance to Japanese, German, or Russian munitions production.

subfiles.title: Division of Controls memorandum recording Campbell’s visit
subfiles.about: Records A. F. Campbell’s delivery of Timken’s statement on export policy.
subfiles.summary: Campbell left the attached Timken letter so the company’s attitude toward exports would be formally recorded. Exton understood that comparable copies were delivered to Colonel MacMorland and Commander Harrison.

subfiles.title: Timken confirmation that sales to Japan and Russia had stopped
subfiles.from: W. E. Umstattd, Timken Roller Bearing Company
subfiles.about: Confirms that Timken had ordered an end to shipments to Japanese and Russian customers.
subfiles.summary: Umstattd states that Timken had considered the national-defense implications before receiving the recipient’s March 14 letter. On March 10 the company instructed its sales departments to discontinue all sales and shipments to Japanese and Russian customers.

subfiles.title: Schober letter protesting Philippine exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges action against shipments from the Philippine Islands to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Schober cites a letter from Woodbury Willoughby in Manila stating that the President’s export order did not prohibit certain Philippine shipments to Japan. She asks Welles to help stop the traffic immediately.

subfiles.title: Reply explaining that the Export Control Act did not apply to the Philippines
subfiles.from: Department of State, by direction of Sumner Welles
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits on applying U.S. export controls to the Philippine Islands.
subfiles.summary: The Department acknowledges Schober’s concern over Philippine shipments to Japan. It explains that the Export Control Act of July 2, 1940 applied to exports from the United States but not the Philippines, and that new legislation would be needed to extend it there.

subfiles.title: Green memorandum on proposed jute-bag shipments
subfiles.about: Records General Maxwell’s decision not to stop imminent jute-bag shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green discussed British reports of jute exports with General Maxwell, who had received similar information from the Waste Bag Dealers Association. Maxwell concluded that domestic jute-bag supplies were not scarce and would not interfere with shipments leaving immediately. Green noted that jute would come under export control on March 24.

subfiles.title: Yost memorandum reporting British figures for jute shipments
subfiles.about: Reports quantities of jute bags being loaded for Japan at four U.S. ports.
subfiles.summary: British consular reports listed 485 tons at Seattle, 645 tons at San Francisco, 150 tons at Portland, and 3,454 bales at New Orleans. The Waste Bag Dealers Association feared the exports would seriously jeopardize U.S. supplies and took the issue to General Maxwell.

subfiles.title: Welles routing note assigning the Fuller letter
subfiles.about: Directs Hamilton to answer Henry M. Fuller’s protest letter.
subfiles.summary: Welles refers the incoming correspondence to Hamilton. He asks Hamilton to prepare the Department’s response.

subfiles.title: Fuller letter protesting arms and strategic exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an embargo on materials that could support Japan’s war effort.
subfiles.summary: Fuller condemns continued exports of cotton, scrap iron, fabricated metals, gasoline, and aircraft-related materials to Japan. He argues that the policy contradicts support for China and Britain and is opposed by many servicemen and citizens. Citing Senators Tobey, White, and Bridges, he asks Welles to press Roosevelt and Hull for an embargo.

subfiles.title: Hamilton reply to Fuller on export-control policy
subfiles.about: Explains the legal and administrative basis of U.S. export controls.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Fuller’s criticism and describes the authority granted by the Export Control Act of July 2, 1940. Decisions on commodities were made by the Administrator of Export Control with advice from interested agencies. He assures Fuller that the Department continually reviewed international conditions while acting within U.S. law and public policy.

subfiles.title: Philadelphia Customs report on abnormal lard shipments to Japan
subfiles.from: G. S. Peffall, Assistant Collector of Customs, Philadelphia
subfiles.about: Reports more than 1.2 million pounds of refined lard booked for Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: Two export declarations covered 15,135 crates and 300 barrels of pure refined lard for loading aboard the Japanese motor ship Nako Maru. Mitsubishi Shoji Kaisha was named as shipper, Cudahy Packing Company as supplier, and Yokohama as the ultimate destination. Customs flagged the transaction as an abnormal movement to Japan.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment of the Philadelphia Customs report
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Thanks Customs for reporting abnormal exports and requests similar future information.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that the reported shipments were receiving appropriate consideration. It asks the collector to continue submitting information about unusual exports observed at Philadelphia.

subfiles.title: Transmission of the Philadelphia lard report to the Export Control Administrator
subfiles.about: Forwards the Customs report on abnormal shipments destined for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green transmits a copy of the Philadelphia collector’s March 20 letter for the administrator’s information. The memorandum highlights the abnormal character of shipments whose stated ultimate destination was Japan.

subfiles.title: Export Control Administrator’s acknowledgment of the Philadelphia report
subfiles.from: Russell L. Maxwell, Administrator of Export Control
subfiles.to: Chief, Division of Controls, Department of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges receipt of the report on Philadelphia shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Maxwell thanks the Division of Controls for forwarding the Philadelphia collector’s March 20 report. The document identifies the subject simply as shipments to Japan.

subfiles.title: Confidential letter to the Maritime Commission on tanker employment
subfiles.from: Breckinridge Long, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Suggests redirecting American-owned foreign-flag tankers toward trades serving U.S. defense needs.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes a global shortage of tanker tonnage and an apparently excessive use of American-controlled foreign-flag tankers in Pacific trade. It asks the Maritime Commission to consider influencing their employment toward national-defense needs. Any approaches to owners were to remain strictly confidential, informal, and oral.

subfiles.title: Bayard Clark letter asking about gasoline shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests clarification of reports that American gasoline sent to Japan was reaching Germany through Russia.
subfiles.summary: Clark reports that North Carolina businessmen had discussed large gasoline sales to Japan. A petroleum-industry figure alleged that much of the gasoline passed through Russia to Germany, a claim Clark had challenged. He asks Hull for information on both export policy and the alleged diversion route.

subfiles.title: Hull reply to Clark on gasoline export controls
subfiles.about: Assures Clark that controlled gasoline exports harmful to national defense were not being licensed.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that Section 6 of the July 2, 1940 act authorized the President to prohibit or curtail exports in the national-defense interest. Because controls were continually adjusted, he declined to give a fixed policy statement. He nevertheless assured Clark that controlled products, including gasoline, were not permitted to Japan or other destinations when detrimental to national defense.

subfiles.title: Inter-office memorandum on asbestos supplies in Japan
subfiles.about: Recommends obtaining field intelligence on Japan’s asbestos supplies and stockpiles.
subfiles.summary: Available figures indicated that Japan imported substantial crude asbestos and manufactured most finished material domestically. Because the data did not show clearly whether asbestos was critical, Leonard recommended asking foreign representatives about shortages and stockpiles. Canada was identified as Japan’s principal source.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Tokyo requesting asbestos information
subfiles.about: Requests discreet information about Japanese asbestos supplies and shortages.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy was instructed to obtain any available information on sources of asbestos supply and possible shortages. The telegram emphasized discreet inquiry.

subfiles.title: Johnson memorandum on Canadian asbestos restrictions
subfiles.about: Reports Canadian quotas and licensing restrictions on asbestos exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Far Eastern Affairs had no independent information on Japanese asbestos supplies, but Johnson favored a cable to Tokyo. Canada had limited exports to Japan to half the previous five-year level and refused licenses for the best grades. Canadian controls may have been weakened by continuing asbestos exports from the United States and by differing commodity definitions.

subfiles.title: Grew telegram on Japan’s asbestos shortage
subfiles.about: Reports very low Japanese stocks of crude asbestos, particularly military grades.
subfiles.summary: Japan was believed to hold only 5,000–7,000 tons of crude asbestos, enough for two or three months, after importing about 23,300 tons in 1940. Canada supplied most imports and was sharply restricting finer grades, while transport problems impeded African shipments. Embassy sources expected the shortage to worsen, and the Japanese Army had taken over all long-fiber stocks.

subfiles.title: Yost transmission of asbestos intelligence to Export Control
subfiles.about: Forwards the Tokyo Embassy’s asbestos report and a Canadian note on export policy.
subfiles.summary: Yost responds to a request from Sanger of the Planning Division. He transmits a paraphrase of Grew’s telegram and a Canadian Legation note describing Canadian policy toward asbestos exports to the Far East.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Grew’s asbestos telegram
subfiles.about: File copy paraphrasing the Embassy’s report on Japan’s asbestos stocks and sources.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase estimates Japanese crude-asbestos stocks at 5,000–7,000 tons and 1940 imports at 23,300 tons, chiefly from Canada. It reports Canadian licensing restrictions, Army seizure of long-fiber stocks, negligible yen-bloc production, and transport barriers to supplies from Rhodesia, South Africa, and Mozambique. A more detailed despatch was being prepared.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning mining interests and ore deposits
subfiles.about: References a memorandum concerning a mining company and ore deposits in the Philippines.
subfiles.summary: The OCR obscures most of the subject, but it appears to mention a company styled Chrome or Iron Mines, Inc. and associated ore deposits. The original memorandum was filed under 811b.6351/10.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to Senator Morris Sheppard’s letter on shipments
subfiles.about: References a letter concerning shipments that might fall under export restrictions.
subfiles.summary: The subject line is badly degraded but refers to material in a letter about shipments potentially coming under a specified control or prohibition. The original was filed under 861.24/467.

subfiles.title: Despatch on toluol aboard the scuttled Atlas
subfiles.from: Josephus Daniels, U.S. Embassy, Mexico City
subfiles.about: Reports the condition and likely disposition of toluol aboard the Italian ship Atlas at Tampico.
subfiles.summary: The toluol was stored aboard the Atlas, which its captain scuttled on April 1, but the ship retained enough freeboard that the tank cargo was probably undamaged. Purchase was considered difficult because the Mexican government wanted toluol for its TNT factory. If Mexico took over the cargo, the material would probably go directly to that factory rather than the market.

subfiles.title: Instruction to Mexico City regarding aluminum intended for Dairen
subfiles.about: Directs efforts to keep six tons of aluminum in Mexico instead of allowing shipment to Dairen.
subfiles.summary: The Embassy was asked to approach the Mexican Foreign Office and American officials of La Consolidada about using the aluminum within Mexico. The Department noted its recent special efforts to secure U.S. aluminum for the Mexican War Department. Those efforts were presented as grounds for asking Mexico to preserve aluminum already within its borders.

subfiles.title: Shipstead letter forwarding a constituent’s protest over exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards Mrs. Samuel Gilmore Dickinson’s letter and requests a report on exports of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Shipstead transmits Dickinson’s protest concerning scrap iron, oil, and other materials allegedly still being sold to Japan. He asks Hull for a report and requests the return of her enclosed letter.

subfiles.title: Dickinson letter demanding an end to war-material exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Calls for an immediate halt to exports of scrap iron, oil, and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Dickinson argues that supplying Japan amounts to arming a probable enemy and that a firm stand might halt further Japanese expansion. She compares U.S. inaction to Britain and France’s response when Hitler remilitarized the Rhine. She favors accepting the risk of a smaller conflict immediately rather than confronting a stronger Japan later.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Senator Shipstead on war-material exports
subfiles.about: Explains licensing controls over scrap iron, petroleum products, and other strategic exports.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that iron and steel scrap, aviation fuel, lubricants, and many other products required special export licenses. Licenses were denied whenever a proposed export was considered detrimental to national defense. It adds that controls were continually revised and extended to new commodities as conditions changed.

subfiles.title: Tokyo telegram on German goods entering Manchuria
subfiles.about: Lists German industrial and military-related equipment recently delivered to Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: A reliable source reported shipments including coal-cutting machinery, Bosch magnetos, locomotives, caterpillar trucks, Heinkel and Junkers aircraft, aircraft engines, torpedo speedboats, drilling equipment, artillery tractors, trucks, and airplane-factory machinery. The deliveries were organized by periods from January through March 1941. The message was routed through Shanghai and circulated confidentially to military-intelligence offices.
